Photograph: George Walker IV/AP Tennessee Justin Pearson and Brent Taylor win primaries for key Tennessee House seat Nominees to face off in November in redistricted seat central to Trump’s bid to retain slim Republican majority Associated Press and Guardian staff Thu 6 Aug 2026 22.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tennessee primary voters picked a pair of Memphis-area lawmakers to square off in a dramatically reconfigured US House seat central to Donald Trump’s plan to try to hold on to a slim Republican majority in the midterm congressional elections. Republicans chose state senator Brent Taylor, who was endorsed by Trump, to be their nominee in the revamped 9th congressional district. Democrats picked state representative Justin Pearson, who gained national prominence three years ago when he was expelled from the Tennessee House for protesting in support of gun control measures. The previously compact Memphis-based district had a majority Black population, but it was cracked apart by Republican officials this year following a US supreme court ruling that weakened federal Voting Rights Act protection for minorities. Republicans hope the redistricting, which is part of a broader national plan pushed by Trump, could give them a clean sweep of all nine of Tennessee’s seats. The new ninth district stretches about 200 miles (320km) east from Memphis across rural areas before reaching north toward Nashville. It previously favored Democrats but now tilts Republican, with 71% of voters new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. Some Memphis voters have raised concerns that their representation has been diminished. The redistricting also significantly reshaped the fifth congressional district held by Republican representative Andy Ogles, who was defeated by the former Tennessee agriculture commissioner Charlie Hatcher. Hatcher prevailed even though Trump gave an early endorsement to Ogles. Ogles’s defeat is a rare loss for Trump, who has backed mostly winners so far in this year’s GOP primaries. Although he lacked the president’s endorsement, Hatcher was endorsed by Republican governor Bill Lee, under whom he had served. Hatcher campaigned as pro-Trump while emphasizing his farming background. “Think what President Trump could do if our congressman spent less time talking and more time doing,” his campaign website said. Ogles, a member of the conservative Freedom Caucus, has faced controversy. The FBI seized his cellphone in 2024 as part of an investigation into his campaign finance reporting. The justice department recently agreed to return the device , signaling that it was abandoning the investigation, which began under the Biden administration. For decades Memphis, the most populous city in Shelby county, formed the base of its own congressional district. Now the county is split among three districts that extend outward like spokes into rural areas. Previously centered on Nashville and central Tennessee, the district now extends to the northwest corner of the state before snaking south along the Mississippi River to Memphis. Along the way it touches the borders of Kentucky, Missouri, Arkansas and Mississippi. In other Tennessee races on Thursday, senator Marsha Blackburn defeated Rose in the GOP primary to succeed Republican governor Bill Lee, who is barred by term limits from seeking reelection. Blackburn, who won her second six-year Senate term in 2024, would have to give the seat up if elected. Memphis city council member Jerri Green won the Democratic gubernatorial primary. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Sydney Newborn baby’s body found in Sydney rubbish bin as police hold ‘serious concerns’ for mother Police urge mother to attend hospital after baby’s body discovered in Harrow Road in Auburn Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Taylor Mon 31 Aug 2026 03.35 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 01.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whose body was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburn in Sydney’s west on Monday morning. Police said emergency services responded to reports of the body of a baby located in a rubbish bin at a unit block along Harrow Road in Auburn at 11.20am, with officers from the Auburn police area command finding the body of a newborn boy. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Acting superintendent of the Auburn area police command, Darren Sly, told reporters that the baby’s body was discovered by a local resident putting out the rubbish. The baby was unclothed and was in a plastic rubbish bag, Sly said. “It’s a sad set of circumstances,” Sly said. “Our number one priority and our number one concern is that of the mother.” A crime scene has been established and detectives have commenced an investigation into the incident. Police said they hold “serious concerns” for the welfare of the baby’s mother, and have urged the mother to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care. Sly told 2GB radio it was believed the baby was born in the past 36 hours, but the body will need to be examined more thoroughly. https://www.berkshireeagle.com/history/e.text: ADVERTISEMENT From the Sept. 21, 1973, Eagle Eagle Archives, Sept. 21, 1973: You've gotta have heart in International Trials Jeannie Maschino Jeannie Maschino Community News Editor / Librarian Published monday, September 21, 2026 - 12:01 a.m. Pavel Kroupa planned to give a party for 40 friends back home in South Africa if he won the bronze medal in the International Six-Days Motorcycle Trials here this week. He envisioned a celebration for 50 people if he won the silver and for 100 if he took the gold medal. He also planned a small party if he was listed at least among the finishers. But plans of South Africa's only contestant in the race will probably be a little less lavish. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT On Monday, the first day of the race, Kroupa's back brakes failed after he reached the second of 13 checkpoints along the 209-mile trail. He rode on, however. At the ninth checkpoint, he pulled off and dropped out. "You must be crazy," he recalls telling himself. "You risk your life for no chance at the bronze." Numerous riders had passed him. He had fallen three times — once ending up with another motorcyclist accidently running over him and stopping on his neck. He lost too much time, he figured, to stop and repair what turned out to be failure of the brake lining. "It was good experience," said Kroupa, Tuesday afternoon. He sat drinking a beer in the Eastover room that he is sharing with his friend and mechanic Josef Smrcka. ADVERTISEMENT Maybe the fault was the manufacturer's, maybe his own, or maybe just bad luck, Kroupa said, mulling it over. The 32-year-old native of Czechoslovakia who moved to South Africa five years ago, Kroupa was already thinking about next year's race, about entering a South African team as other nations did this year, and about better preparation. He figured it cost $3,000 for him to order a Penton-KTM 125cc motorcycle from South Africa, to have it delivered here only three days before the race and for him to travel here. He and Josef are on a month's leave from a small engineering firm in Johannesburg. On Sunday night in an interview before the race, he was nervous, thinking of the race and trying not to. "This sport you must do with your heart," he said. "This is experience of years. This is not something you learn in a month or two months. It was his first trial race in more than 10 years.
